title: De Fato
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero

passages.original: Etenim si illud vere conectitur: Si oriente Canicula natus es, in mari non moriere, primumque quod est in conexo: Natus es oriente Canicula, necessarium est (omnia enim vera in praeteritis necessaria sunt, ut Chrysippo placet dissentienti a magistro Cleanthe, quia sunt inmutabilia nec in falsum e vero praeterita possunt convertere); si igitur, quod primum in conexo est, necessarium est, fit etiam, quod consequitur, necessarium. Quamquam hoc Chrysippo non videtur valere in omnibus; sed tamen, si naturalis est causa, cur in mari Fabius non moriatur, in mari Fabius mori non potest.
passages.english: For if this conditional is truly connected: "If you were born at the rising of the Dog Star, you will not die at sea," and the first part in the conditional, "You were born at the rising of the Dog Star," is necessary (for all true statements about the past are necessary, as Chrysippus holds, disagreeing with his teacher Cleanthes, because they are unchangeable and past things cannot turn from true into false); if, then, what is first in the conditional is necessary, what follows also becomes necessary. Chrysippus, however, does not think this holds in all cases; but still, if there is a natural cause why Fabius should not die at sea, Fabius cannot die at sea.

passages.original: Hoc loco Chrysippus aestuans falli sperat Chaldaeos ceterosque divinos, neque eos usuros esse coniunctionibus, ut ita sua percepta pronuntient: Si quis natus est oriente Canicula, is in mari non morietur, sed potius ita dicant: Non et natus est quis oriente Canicula, et is in mari morietur. O licentiam iocularem! ne ipse incidat in Diodorum, docet Chaldaeos, quo pacto eos exponere percepta oporteat. Quaero enim, si Chaldaei ita loquantur, ut negationes infinitarum coniunctionum potius quam infinita conexa ponant, cur idem medici, cur geometrae, cur reliqui facere non possint.
passages.english: At this point Chrysippus, in a fever of difficulty, hopes that the Chaldaeans and the other diviners are mistaken, and that they will not use conditionals to state their findings in this way: "If anyone was born at the rising of the Dog Star, he will not die at sea," but should rather say: "It is not the case both that someone was born at the rising of the Dog Star and that he will die at sea." What playful licence! So as not to fall in with Diodorus himself, he teaches the Chaldaeans how they ought to set out their findings. For I ask: if the Chaldaeans were to speak so as to lay down negations of indefinite conjunctions rather than indefinite conditionals, why could not doctors, geometers and the rest do the same?

passages.original: Hic primum si mihi libeat adsentiri Epicuro et negare omnem enuntiationem aut veram esse aut falsam, eam plagam potius accipiam quam fato omnia fieri conprobem; illa enim sententia habet aliquid disputationis, haec vero non est tolerabilis. Itaque contendit omnis nervos Chrysippus, ut persuadeat omne a)ci/wma aut verum esse aut falsum. Ut enim Epicurus veretur, ne, si hoc concesserit, concedendum sit fato fieri, quaecumque fiant, (si enim alterum utrum ex aeternitate verum sit, esse id etiam certum et, si certum, etiam necessarium; ita et necessitatem et fatum confirmari putat) sic Chrysippus metuit, ne, si non obtinuerit omne, quod enuntietur, aut verum esse aut falsum, non teneat omnia fato fieri et ex causis aeternis rerum futurarum.
passages.english: Here, first, if I should choose to agree with Epicurus and deny that every proposition is either true or false, I would rather take that blow than approve that everything happens by fate; for that view admits of some argument, but this one is truly intolerable. So Chrysippus strains every nerve to persuade us that every axiōma [proposition] is either true or false. For just as Epicurus fears that, if he grants this, he must grant that whatever happens happens by fate (for if one or the other is true from eternity, it is also certain, and if certain, also necessary; thus he thinks both necessity and fate are established), so Chrysippus fears that, if he does not maintain that everything stated is either true or false, he cannot hold that all things happen by fate and from eternal causes of future events.
passages.notes: Greek axiōma printed in Beta-code transliteration in the source.

passages.original: Sed Epicurus declinatione atomi vitari necessitatem fati putat. Itaque tertius quidam motus oritur extra pondus et plagam, cum declinat atomus intervallo minimo (id appellat e)la/- xiston); quam declinationem sine causa fieri si minus verbis, re cogitur confiteri.
passages.english: But Epicurus thinks the necessity of fate is avoided by the swerve of the atom. So a certain third motion arises besides weight and impact, when the atom swerves by the smallest interval (this he calls elachiston [the least]); and he is compelled, if not in words, then in fact, to admit that this swerve happens without a cause.
passages.notes: Greek elachiston split by line break and given in Beta-code in the source.

passages.original: Ex hoc genere illud est Ennii: Utinám ne in nemore Pélio secúribus Caesae áccidissent ábiegnae ad terrám trabes! Licuit vel altius: Utinam ne in Pelio nata ulla umquam esset arbor! etiam supra: Utinam ne esset mons ullus Pelius!
passages.english:
Of this kind is that [passage] of Ennius:
"Would that in the Pelian grove the fir-wood beams,
cut down by axes, had never fallen to the earth!"
One could [go back] even further: "Would that no tree had ever been born on Pelion!" And even further back: "Would that there were no Mount Pelion at all!"
passages.notes: The accent marks in the quotation (Utinám, Pélio, etc.) are the edition's metrical ictus marks, not part of the words. The Ennius lines are the opening of his Medea, adapted from Euripides.

passages.original: Quam ob rem, qui ita fatum introducunt, ut necessitatem adiungant, in eos valebit illa conclusio; qui autem causas antecedentis non dicent perfectas neque principalis, in eos nihil valebit. Quod enim dicantur adsensiones fieri causis antepositis, id quale sit, facile a se explicari putat. Nam quamquam adsensio non possit fieri nisi commota viso, tamen, cum id visum proximam causam habeat, non principalem, hanc habet rationem, ut Chrysippus vult, quam dudum diximus, non ut illa quidem fieri possit nulla vi extrinsecus excitata (necesse est enim adsensionem viso commoveri), sed revertitur ad cylindrum et ad turbinem suum, quae moveri incipere nisi pulsa non possunt. Id autem cum accidit, suapte natura, quod superest, et cylindrum volvi et versari turbinem putat.
passages.english: Therefore that conclusion will hold against those who introduce fate in such a way as to attach necessity to it; but against those who will not call the antecedent causes complete and principal, it will have no force. For what it means that assents are said to come about through prior causes, he thinks he can easily explain. For although assent cannot occur unless prompted by an impression, yet since that impression has a proximate cause, not a principal one, it works in the way Chrysippus wants, as we said a while ago: not that assent can indeed occur with no force arousing it from outside (for assent must be prompted by an impression), but he returns to his cylinder and his spinning top, which cannot begin to move unless struck. But once that happens, he thinks that for the rest the cylinder rolls and the top spins by their own nature.
passages.notes: This passage appears to be an excerpt; 'he thinks' refers to Chrysippus.

passages.original: Hoc modo hanc causam disceptari oportet, non ab atomis errantibus et de via declinantibus petere praesidium. Declinat, inquit, atomus. Primum cur? aliam enim quandam vim motus habebant a Democrito inpulsionis, quam plagam ille appellat, a te, Epicure, gravitatis et ponderis. Quae ergo nova causa in natura est, quae declinet atomum? aut num sortiuntur inter se, quae declinet, quae non? aut cur minimo declinent intervallo, maiore non?
passages.english: This is how this case ought to be argued, not by seeking protection from atoms that wander and swerve from their path. "The atom swerves," he says. First, why? For they had a certain other force of motion: from Democritus, that of impulsion, which he calls impact; from you, Epicurus, that of gravity and weight. What new cause, then, is there in nature to make the atom swerve? Or do they draw lots among themselves as to which will swerve and which not? Or why do they swerve by the smallest interval and not a larger one?

passages.original: Itaque M. Cicero in libro, quem de fato conscripsit, cum quaestionem istam diceret obscurissimam esse et inplicatissimam, Chrysippum quoque philosophum non expedisse se in ea ait his verbis Chrysippus aestuans laboransque, quonam pacto explicet et fato omnia fieri, et esse aliquid in nobis, intricatur hoc modo.
passages.english: And so Marcus Cicero, in the book he wrote on fate, while saying that this question was most obscure and most entangled, says that the philosopher Chrysippus too did not extricate himself from it, in these words: "Chrysippus, in a fever of difficulty and labouring over how he may explain both that everything happens by fate and that something is in our power, entangles himself in this way."
passages.notes: A testimonium from a later author (Gellius) quoting Cicero, not Cicero's own text.

passages.original: Cicero dicit Hippocratem, nobilissimum medicum, scriptum reliquisse quosdam fratres, cum simul aegrotare coepissent et eorum morbus eodem tempore ingravesceret, eodem levaretur, geminos suspicatum. quos Posidonius Stoicus multum astrologiae deditus eadem constitutione astrorum natos eademque conceptos solebat asserere.
passages.english: Cicero says that Hippocrates, the most famous physician, left it in writing that he suspected certain brothers to be twins, since they had begun to fall ill at the same time and their illness grew worse at the same time and eased at the same time. Posidonius the Stoic, much given to astrology, used to assert that they had been born under the same configuration of the stars and conceived under the same.
passages.notes: A testimonium (Augustine, City of God 5.2) reporting Cicero.
